definitions.definition: The Land of Peace and Bliss (Anle, Anyang, Jile) of Amitābha, west beyond ten trillion buddha-lands; not included in the three realms; made by Dharmākara's vows; those born there are non-retrogressive.
Gokuraku, the Pure Land of Amida; the true land of immeasurable light, where birth is at once the attainment of nirvāṇa; distinct from its transformed (provisional) lands.

cross_language.native: 極樂 / 安樂 / 安養

definitions.definition: Recollecting Amitābha — contemplating his marks or land, or calling his name; from Shandao onward chiefly the oral calling of 'Namo Amituofo' as the rightly determined act.
Nenbutsu: saying 'Namu Amida Butsu' with the conviction of being born; the practice selected in the primal vow.
Nenbutsu: the name of Amida transferred to beings; in the person of shinjin it is an expression of gratitude, 'neither practice nor good' for the practitioner.
Nenbutsu in which the name itself is birth, recited and danced having cast off self.

cross_language.note: the Indian term means recollection; East Asian usage came to mean calling the name

definitions.definition: Recollection of Amitābha in samādhi (pratyutpanna, Contemplation Sūtra) or by calling his name; Daochuo calls the samādhi of recollection the king of samādhis.
Non-retrogression: reached quickly by the easy path of faith (Nāgārjuna); assured to all born in Sukhāvatī for five reasons (Jingtu shiyi lun); Tanluan equates it with the rightly established group.
Attained in this life at the moment of shinjin ('immediately attain birth and dwell in non-retrogression').
The aspiration to become a buddha, which is the aspiration to save beings (Tanluan); required of all three grades; Shandao's and later Chinese teachers keep it with recitation.
Not required as a separate condition of birth in Hōnen's reading of the three grades (a point Myōe attacked).
The other-power aspiration for awakening, crosswise transcending: it is shinjin itself, given by Amida.
In Tanluan two dharma-bodies: of dharma-nature and of expedient means, different but inseparable; the Rebirth Treatise's 'uncreated dharma-body of true wisdom'.
The formless dharma-body as suchness from which Dharmākara appeared; Amida is the means to know jinen.
Dharma-nature (faxing), pure and ultimately unborn; 'birth' is said only from the side of those born (Tanluan, Daochuo).

The five grave offences (wuni): excluded, with slander of the Dharma, in the eighteenth vow; yet the Contemplation Sūtra admits five-offence evil-doers to the lowest grade; Tanluan and Shandao reconcile the two.
Buddha-nature is great shinjin; buddha-nature is the Tathāgata (Jōdo wasan, quoting the Nirvāṇa Sūtra).
Transfer of merit (huixiang), fifth of the five gates; of two aspects, going (to be born with all beings) and returning (to teach them) (Tanluan).
Ekō is Amida's transfer of his merit to beings, not the practitioner's; the nenbutsu is 'non-transferring' practice for the practitioner.
Bonnō, blind passions: the foolish being is 'fully possessed of blind passions' (bonnō gusoku) to the end of life; the vow is for such a being; lack of joy in the nenbutsu is their working.
Faith (xin): 'if one plants good roots but doubts, the lotus does not open; with pure faith it opens'; faith is the source of the way (Wang Rixiu); the first of Ouyi's three provisions.

literal: Pure Land that is only mind

definitions.definition: The Pure Land as mind only, affirmed by Yanshou, Tianru and Zhuhong together with real birth in the West: the mind-only land is born only when the mind is understood; to purify the mind there is no method apart from Pure Land practice.
Rejected as a reading of the Pure Land: Shandao's 'pointing to a direction and establishing form' holds the Western land to be real for ordinary beings.
The 'single mind' of Vasubandhu's opening verse ('with single mind I take refuge'); in Tanluan the undivided faith that accords with reality.
Isshin: the one mind into which the three minds of the eighteenth vow are gathered, i.e. true shinjin.
The buddha of immeasurable light (and life), Dharmākara after fulfilling his vows, presiding over Sukhāvatī; the object of recollection and calling.
Amida Nyorai, the Tathāgata of Unhindered Light filling the ten directions; the means by which the formless reality (jinen) is made known.
Immeasurable Life, the other name of the same buddha, used in the Contemplation Sūtra and the Sanskrit sūtras; Chinese Wuliangshou.
A pure land — a buddha-field purified by a buddha's vows; above all Amitābha's land in the West.
Jōdo: the Western Land to which the nenbutsu practitioner is born at death.

cross_language.note: no single Sanskrit equivalent of the Chinese compound

equivalents.note: a pure land is a purified buddha-field

literal: homage to Amida Buddha; I take refuge in Amida Buddha

definitions.definition: The six-character name: to say it with the conviction of birth is the whole of the nenbutsu.
The name in which the person and the Dharma are one; the working of the vow calling the being; object of reverence (myōgō honzon).
The name that is itself birth, settled for all beings ten kalpas ago; printed on the talismans.
Namo Amituofo, the six-character name recited in Chinese Pure Land (four-character 'Amituofo' in quick recitation).
The Buddha's name (and title): Amitābha's name, which all buddhas praise (17th vow) and which beings call.
Myōgō: the name in which all the Buddha's virtues are gathered (Senchakushū 3).
Calling (vocally reciting) the Buddha's name; for Shandao the rightly determined act, easy for beings whose minds are too coarse for contemplation.
Shōmyō: saying the name, the great practice (Kyōgyōshinshō, Gyō); for the person of shinjin, gratitude.
The samādhi of recollecting the Buddha, in which one sees him (pratyutpanna; Contemplation Sūtra 9); king of samādhis (Daochuo); readily attained by loud recitation (Huaigan).

The 'ten recitations' of the eighteenth vow and of the lowest grade: ten continuous thoughts of recollection without other thoughts, not needing to be counted (Tanluan, Daochuo); ten voicings of the name (Shandao); ten breaths of continuous recitation each morning (Zunshi).

cross_language.note: Sanskrit vow 19: 'ten turnings of the arising of thought'

definitions.definition: 'One thought': hearing the name and rejoicing even for one thought gains the great benefit (Larger Sūtra); one calling removes eighty koṭis of kalpas of sin (Daochuo).
Ichinen: the one thought-moment of shinjin, 'the ultimate brevity of time', and the one calling that follows.
The original (primal) vow of Amitābha, above all the eighteenth; its power is the dominant condition of birth (Tanluan).
Hongan: the eighteenth vow, which selected the nenbutsu.

equivalents.note: a buddha's past vow as bodhisattva

definitions.definition: The power of the original vow, which 'lets none who meet it pass in vain' (Vasubandhu).
Hongan-riki: the other-power of Amida's vow on which the person of shinjin wholly relies.
Other-power (tali): the power of the Buddha's vow as the dominant condition of birth; the easy path rides on it like a lame man on a ship (Tanluan).
Birth by the Buddha's power, through the nenbutsu that accords with the vow.
Other-power is Amida's primal vow-power; the practitioner's 'no working' is true working; shinjin itself is other-power.

equivalents.note: both name salvation by the power of another (the Buddha's vow / the Lord's grace); the Pure Land tradition does not posit a creator Lord

definitions.definition: Self-power (zili): reliance on one's own practice to reach non-retrogression, the difficult path.
Reliance on one's own good and one's own calculation, including self-power nenbutsu (20th vow); leads to the transformed land.
Going to be born (in the Pure Land) at death — the 'birth of non-birth' from the vow, the condition for completing awakening.
Ōjō: birth in the true land at death, which is at once attaining nirvāṇa; settled at the moment of shinjin.
The 'birth of non-birth': birth in the Pure Land arises from the pure vow and is not the deluded birth of the three existences (Tanluan, quoted by Daochuo).
The easy practice: reaching non-retrogression by faith and calling the buddhas' names (Nāgārjuna), by riding the Buddha's vow (Tanluan).
The difficult practice: seeking non-retrogression by strenuous self-power effort in an age without a buddha.
The gate of the holy path: attaining awakening in this world by one's own practice; hard to realise in the last age (Daochuo).
Shōdōmon: to be set aside in favour of the Pure Land gate (Senchakushū 1).
The Pure Land gate: birth in Amitābha's land, the only gate passable in the last age (Daochuo).
The last age of the Dharma, when the teaching remains but practice and realization do not; Daochuo places his own time in the fourth five-hundred-year period.
Mappō: the present age, in which only nominal monks remain and only Amida's vow saves.

equivalents.note: the Indian sūtras speak of the disappearance of the true Dharma; the three-age scheme with a 'final' age is East Asian

definitions.definition: The age of the true Dharma after the Buddha's passing, when teaching, practice and realization are present.
The age of the semblance Dharma, when teaching and practice remain without realization.
The five turbidities (wuzhuo) — of the kalpa, views, passions, beings and life-span — marking this evil world in which only the Pure Land gate is passable.
Slander (rejection) of the true Dharma (bangfa), excluded with the five grave offences from the eighteenth vow; graver than the offences because it rejects the very Dharma (Tanluan).

The rightly established group (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi): those assured of awakening; those born in Sukhāvatī dwell in it (11th vow); Nāgārjuna's 'stage of certainty' (biding) entered by recollecting Amitābha.
Shōjōju: entered in this life at the moment of shinjin, not first in the Pure Land.
The three minds of the Contemplation Sūtra — sincere, deep, and dedicating-aspiring — which Shandao makes the settled mind for birth.
Shinran distinguishes these (self-power, of the Contemplation Sūtra) from the three minds of the eighteenth vow, which are one mind given by Amida.
The sincere mind: true in worship, praise and contemplation, without outward show and inward falsehood (Shandao).
The deep mind, true entrusting, of two kinds: in oneself as an ordinary being without escape, and in Amitābha's vow (Shandao).

literal: mind of dedicating merit and aspiring

definitions.definition: The mind that dedicates all roots of good and aspires to birth (Shandao).
The two kinds of deep entrusting: concerning the person (ki) — oneself as a sinful ordinary being — and concerning the Dharma (hō) — Amitābha's vow that surely saves.
Nishu jinshin (ki no jinshin, hō no jinshin), the structure of shinjin.
The settled mind — the three minds — with which the nenbutsu is said; the first of anjin, kigyō, sagyō (from Shandao's 安心起行作業).
The settled mind of other-power shinjin (Rennyo's usage).
The four modes of practice: reverent, exclusive, uninterrupted and long-lasting (Shandao).
The five right practices directed to Amitābha: reciting the sūtras, contemplating, worshipping, calling the name, praising and offering (Shandao).
The rightly determined act: calling Amitābha's name single-heartedly at all times, because it accords with his vow (Shandao).
Shōjōgō: the calling of the name, to be chosen over the auxiliary acts (Senchakushū 16).
The name of the primal vow is the act of right assurance; shinjin is its cause (Shōshinge).
The auxiliary acts: the four right practices other than calling the name.
Miscellaneous practices: all good practices not directed exclusively to Amitābha.
Zōgyō: to be cast aside (Senchakushū 2).
Exclusive practice: 'ten of ten are born'; mixed practice rarely succeeds (Shandao; Huaigan).
Exclusive nenbutsu: calling the name alone as the practice for birth; the name of Hōnen's movement.
Selection: Dharmākara selected the nenbutsu in the primal vow; Śākyamuni and all buddhas selected it in the sūtras; so the practitioner selects it (Senchakushū).

notes: Read senjaku in Jōdo-shū, senchaku in Shinshū.

definitions.definition: The 'one-calling' position associated with Kōsai: birth is settled by a single calling or single thought of faith.
The 'many-calling' position associated with Ryūkan: continued lifelong calling is needed.
True entrusting: the mind free of doubt about the primal vow, given (transferred) by Amida; the true cause of birth, buddha-nature itself, arising in one thought-moment and settling birth.

cross_language.note: in Chinese texts ordinary 'faith'; in Shinran a technical term

equivalents.note: Shinshū insists shinjin is not the practitioner's faith but the Buddha's mind given; general Buddhist śraddhā is a faculty of the practitioner

literal: transfer in the aspect of going

definitions.definition: The going aspect of transfer: dedicating merit to be born with all beings (Tanluan).
Amida's transfer by which beings go to the Pure Land: teaching, practice, shinjin, realization.

literal: transfer in the aspect of returning

definitions.definition: The returning aspect: having been born, returning to birth-and-death to teach beings (Tanluan; fifth gate).
Also Amida's gift, from the twenty-second vow.
The five gates of mindfulness of the Rebirth Treatise: worship, praise, aspiration, contemplation, transfer.
The 'one dharma-phrase', the pure phrase, the uncreated dharma-body of true wisdom, into which the 29 adornments enter (Vasubandhu).

literal: the evil person is the proper recipient

definitions.definition: The evil person as the true object of the vow: 'even a good person attains birth, how much more an evil person'.

literal: naturalness, thus by virtue of the Dharma

definitions.definition: Being so of itself by the working of the vow, without the practitioner's calculation; the formless supreme Buddha is jinen (Shinran's letter).
Calculation, the practitioner's own designing and judging; 'no working (no calculation) is true working'.
'Neither monk nor layman': Shinran's self-description after being laicised in 1207.
'Foolish bald-head', the name Shinran took after exile; expresses the self as foolish ordinary being.

literal: turning and entering through the three vows

definitions.definition: Turning through the three vows: from the nineteenth (various goods) through the twentieth (self-power nenbutsu) to the eighteenth (other-power shinjin) (Kyōgyōshinshō, Transformed Lands).
Crosswise transcendence: leaping at once out of birth-and-death by other-power shinjin, not by stages (vertical) practice.

cross_language.note: the Larger Sūtra has 橫截 'cut crosswise'

definitions.definition: Repaying the Buddha's benevolence: the nenbutsu of the person of shinjin is said in gratitude (hōon no nenbutsu).
To rely on (Amida) to save one in the life to come — Rennyo's plain-language expression for shinjin.

literal: the one great matter of the afterlife

definitions.definition: The one great matter of the life to come, which Rennyo urges all to take to heart.
The oneness of the person (ki) and the Dharma (hō) in Namu Amida Butsu (Anjin ketsujōshō; Rennyo).
Past karma, by whose conditions one may do what one would not intend (Tannishō 13).
'Wondrous good person': title for exemplary lay Shinshū devotees (from Shandao's praise of nenbutsu people); later collections record their lives (Akao no Dōshū; Asahara Saichi).

notes: Shandao glosses the sūtra's puṇḍarīka as 'good person, wondrous good person' among people (recalled).

definitions.definition: Itinerant holy man outside the monastic establishment who spread the nenbutsu (Kūya, the Kōya and Bessho hijiri, Ippen).
Dancing nenbutsu, recitation with rhythmic dancing and drum, begun by Ippen in 1279.
Distributing slips printed 'Namu Amida Butsu — birth assured — six hundred thousand people' to all, without regard to faith or purity.
'Only by casting away': Kūya's word as quoted by Ippen — casting off wisdom, good and evil, even the wish for the Pure Land, and simply saying the name.
The interfusing nenbutsu: each person's recitation interpenetrates all others' (one is all, all is one).
The welcoming descent: Amitābha with the bodhisattvas and assembly appears to the dying practitioner (19th vow; Smaller Sūtra).
Belongs to birth by various practices; the person of shinjin need not await it.
Deathbed rites: placing the dying before an image of Amitābha facing west, the five-coloured cord, recitation and attendants' guidance (Genshin, after Shandao and Daoxuan).

literal: right mindfulness at the end of life

definitions.definition: Right mindfulness at death: dying with an unconfused mind fixed on Amitābha, the aim of deathbed practice.
Assisting recitation: companions recite the name for and with the dying so that ten recitations are completed (Daochuo; Yinguang).
Womb-birth: those who aspire with doubt of the Buddha's wisdom dwell five hundred years in closed palaces or lotuses without seeing the Buddha.
Taishō: birth in the transformed land of self-power practitioners.
Transformation (apparitional) birth, seated in a lotus, of those who trust the Buddha's wisdom.
The borderland of the Pure Land, another name for womb-birth (Tanluan).
The land (realm) of sloth and pride west of here, where those of mixed practice stop (Huaigan, citing the Pusa chutai jing).
Kemangai: one of the names of the transformed land.
Reward land: Sukhāvatī as the land produced by Dharmākara's vows and practice, into which ordinary beings are born by the vow's power (Daochuo, Shandao).
Transformation land: the view (rejected by Daochuo and Shandao) that Sukhāvatī is a manifested land of a transformation-body buddha.
Kedo: the provisional land for those of self-power practice, within the true land's reward.
Ordinary being, not a sage; the Contemplation Sūtra calls even Vaidehī a fanfu, and Shandao holds all nine grades are ordinary beings.
Bonbu: the foolish being full of blind passions to the last moment of life.
'Amitābha of one's own nature': in the Chan-inflected reading every buddha is Amitābha of the original nature (Tianru); held together with birth in the West.
'Intention for another time' (Mahāyānasaṃgraha: kālāntarābhiprāya): the claim that birth by vows or ten recitations comes only in a distant future; refuted by Daochuo and Huaigan.
The 'gate of restraint': Shandao's reading of the eighteenth vow's exclusion as a deterrent, not a rejection.
Embraced and never abandoned: the Buddha's light embraces beings who recollect him (Contemplation Sūtra 9).
Sesshu fusha: the benefit received at the moment shinjin arises (Tannishō 1).
Faith, vow and practice — the three provisions for birth (Ouyi).
The undistracted single mind in holding the name (Smaller Sūtra); in Zhuhong of phenomenal and principled kinds.
The essential gate: Śākyamuni's teaching of meditative and non-meditative good dedicated to birth (Shandao).
The universal vow: Amitābha's great vow by which good and evil ordinary beings are born (Shandao).
Meditative good: the first thirteen contemplations of the Contemplation Sūtra, practised with a concentrated mind.
Non-meditative good: the three meritorious acts and the nine grades (contemplations 14–16), done with an ordinary scattered mind.
The three meritorious acts of the Contemplation Sūtra: worldly virtue, precepts, and Mahāyāna practice with bodhicitta — 'the right cause of the pure acts of all buddhas'.
The white lotus: one who recollects the Buddha is a puṇḍarīka among people (Contemplation Sūtra).
Those who hear and entrust themselves to the vow are called white lotuses (Shōshinge).

literal: acceptance that dharmas do not arise

definitions.definition: The acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas: gained by Vaidehī on seeing the land; gained by those born there; Mahāsthāmaprāpta entered it through recollection.
The practice hall (bodhimaṇḍa) prepared for the nianfo samādhi retreat (Shandao).
